📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta owners. The patch includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Industry observers note that as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

It has been revealed that the redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final upgrade.

It has been revealed that the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-newly introduced design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 owners, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a fresh Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week looks based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo people, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also brings a newly introduced face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a new option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with upcoming clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

In a recent development, this includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

According to recent reports, iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the patch expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these fresh capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

Sources indicate that with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple states it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to upcoming languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

Sources indicate that you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ plan, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

iOS 27.3 is a major revision to Safari. First, the update adds support for a fresh vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

In a recent development, for Apple Music customers, iOS 27.3 adds a latest “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

It has been revealed that there are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

In a recent development, second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a upcoming “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

Here are a few other changes in iOS 27.3:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.
  • Sources indicate that databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
  • In a recent development, the talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.

Sources indicate that databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be nearly 20% above the $190bn valuation the data company reached in August.

In a recent development, the talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal. TNW has not independently verified the report.

It has been revealed that the new money would come while Databricks stays private. Its chief executive, Ali Ghodsi, explained why in a recent interview on the All-In podcast.

Recent findings suggest that “We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now I think during this transition period of AI there’s just too much up and down, and I think it’s distracting to companies,” Ghodsi told All-In.

Databricks closed a $5bn round at $190bn in August. It said then that it had passed a $7bn revenue run rate, the Journal reported.

In a recent development, ghodsi told All-In the business is growing 70% to 80% a year, and that he wants more. He would like growth of 100%, “way over 100”, he said.

The company has added AI products this year. They include an agent called Genie One, which answers questions from a company’s business data, and Unity Gateway, which gives customers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Genie also reached Slack this month, in a version that answers data questions inside the chat app.

Its investors include Coatue Management, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the Journal.

The Journal calls Databricks a candidate for a near-term listing. Investors say a strong showing by Anthropic, whose stock ended its first week worth $1.6tn, could unleash a wave of AI listings, the paper reported.

Ghodsi weighed both sides on All-In. A listing brings access to capital and a quarterly marketing moment, he noted. Staying private means Databricks must arrange its own tender offers for staff every year. He said employees have never used up all the money set aside for them.

It has been revealed that his worry is volatility. When a stock falls, he mentioned, staff effectively take a pay cut, and some leave before the price recovers.

Ghodsi also remarked he believes AI has already reached artificial general intelligence, by the definition his Berkeley lab used around 2010. He put the risk of AI wiping out humanity close to zero, and named cyberattacks as the real danger.

“I think the cyber risk is real and really bad things can happen with that,” he noted.

  • It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar demonstrates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

Industry observers note that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session highlights how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just unveiled the return of one of its most popular series: Presumed Innocent. Here’s the release date and first trailer.

Presumed Innocent, the legal thriller starring Jake Gyllenhaal, was a substantial hit for Apple when it aired in 2024. Though it was originally conceived as a limited series, Apple gave it a surprise renewal for season 2.

The new season won’t feature Gyllenhaal’s character, but instead tells an all-new story with a cast led by Rachel Brosnahan and Matthew Rhys (Widow’s Bay).

Presumed Innocent season 2 premieres Friday, February 19 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases through April 2.

Here’s the official plot summary, followed by the teaser trailer:.

In a recent development, the sophomore season of “Presumed Innocent” is based on “Dissection of a Murder,” the debut legal thriller novel by Jo Murray, who also serves as a co-executive producer. Up-and-coming defense attorney Lelia Reynolds (Brosnahan) faces off against her district attorney husband (Rhys) in a murder case that threatens to destroy both their careers and their marriage.

You can watch Presumed Innocent season 1 on Apple TV. The eight-episode first season tells the story of “the horrific murder that upends the Chicago Prosecuting Attorney’s office when one of its own is suspected of a crime.”.

Apple has started making a habit of renewing reveals that were originally intended as limited series.

It has been revealed that the streamer recently gave season 2 renewals to acclaimed comedy Margo’s Got Money Troubles and thriller Imperfect Women. But Presumed Innocent preceded them both, and it will be interesting to see if its return proves successful.

Apple TV is available for just $6.99 per month (over 50% off) through Monday, November 30.

Samsung names upcoming chip and phone bosses amid a reported China shipment halt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.
  • According to recent reports, samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses.
  • Sources indicate that sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung remarked in a newsroom statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.

According to recent reports, samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The tech giant announced the changes on Friday in Korea.

Sources indicate that sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung remarked in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

Samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung noted it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly plans to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

Industry observers note that sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the launches of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under fresh rules, the FT reported.

According to recent reports, the rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

It has been revealed that samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba said this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

Some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

Recent findings suggest that samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement states it wants the new team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

#39623. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

Industry observers note that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell indicates. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

According to recent reports, the screen indicates my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

Sources indicate that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” claims Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Industry observers note that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team highlighted me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Industry observers note that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

It has been revealed that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga notes. “It was just major enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” claims Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Recent findings suggest that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

In a recent development, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

According to recent reports, in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

According to recent reports, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

According to recent reports, still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

Recent findings suggest that but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more vital than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell indicates. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

According to recent reports, during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” indicates neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, notes experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra notes, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Recent findings suggest that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

It has been revealed that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell states. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell notes. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in upcoming funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he indicates. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga claims they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this newly introduced technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

It has been revealed that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • According to recent reports, macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the manufacturer’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

According to recent reports, macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

I’m a substantial fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, owners had to wait until it “just worked.”.

It has been revealed that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an enhancement, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Recent findings suggest that make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

According to recent reports, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

According to recent reports, it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Recent findings suggest that will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

Sources indicate that I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech people may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sean Williams – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:06AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

According to recent reports, since the 2022 bear market bottomed, it's been all systems go for the ageless Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.93%), benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), and innovation-inspired Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%). Since reaching their respective troughs, the Dow has powered higher by up to 90%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have more than doubled.

Recent findings suggest that while the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out has been the primary catalyst behind Wall Street's gains, it's not the only reason stocks are higher. Historically low peak marginal corporate income tax rates have fueled record share buyback activity by S&P 500 companies. Stock-split euphoria and record-breaking initial public offerings are also intriguing retail investors.

While history has repeatedly shown that the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite rally over multiple decades, it also tells us that bull markets don't last forever. Eventually, something is going to knock Wall Street's AI-driven bull market off its pedestal -- and we may be watching that bubble burst before our very eyes right now.

While everyone's focused on the potential formation and subsequent bursting of an AI bubble, there's a $1.5 trillion bubble that looks to be bursting in real time.

Even though past events can't concretely predict the future, history has a way of rhyming on Wall Street. In other words, historical precedent often sets the tone.

Over the last three decades, few, if any, past events, metrics, or indicators have accurately forecast the future quite like outstanding margin debt.

Margin represents the money an investor borrows, with interest, from their broker to short-sell (wager against) or purchase securities, such as stocks or exchange-traded funds (ETFs). When used to buy stocks or ETFs, margin acts as leverage -- and leverage can be risky.

Industry observers note that on the one hand, if a stock or ETF moves in the desired direction, margin can help an investor amplify their gains. But if the security in question moves in the opposite direction, it can quickly magnify losses, on top of owing the broker interest on what's borrowed. This dynamic is what makes outstanding margin debt a crude but incredibly useful risk-measuring metric.

Over multiple decades, we'd expect outstanding margin debt to rise in lockstep with the cumulative value of the U.S. stock market. But when margin debt rises in parabolic fashion over a short period, things typically break.

Total Margin Debt hits $1.5 Trillion, a new all-time high 🤯 👀 https://t.co/1IXqZGgrqs.

Since 1998, outstanding margin debt has skyrocketed at least 65% over a short timeline on four occasions, the previous three of which were followed by significant stock market declines:.

While the AI revolution is fueling risk-taking, we're witnessing possible evidence of a top. Over the previous four months, outstanding margin debt has fallen from $1.502 trillion to $1.448 trillion, as of October.

When investors lighten up their leverage following a parabolic increase, it's historically been the ultimate red flag for Wall Street and investors that a bubble is about to burst.

Though history doesn't always offer the rosiest of short-term outlooks, historical precedent can change drastically depending on investors' perspectives.

In one respect, corrections and bear markets are par for the course when putting your money to work in the stock market. Given that emotions often drive downturns, there isn't much that can be done from a monetary or fiscal policy perspective to stop these double-digit declines from cropping up.

But these downturns share a theme: they're historically short-lived.

Sources indicate that six months ago, the analysts at wealth management firm Bespoke Investment Group calculated the calendar-day length of every S&P 500 bull and bear market since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929. They uncovered a night-and-day difference between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.

The current bull market that began on 10/12/22 is now the 9th longest in S&P 500 history, surpassing the 1,324-day bull that ended on 2/9/1966: https://t.co/4mGsS2t2ft.

Whereas the typical S&P 500 bear market has lasted just 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months) over the last 97 years, the average bull market has persisted for approximately 3.6 times as long (1,023 calendar days).

Furthermore, no bear market has taken longer than 630 calendar days to find its trough, according to Bespoke. Meanwhile, just over half (14 of 27) of the S&P 500 bull markets since September 1929 have lasted longer than 630 calendar days.

Sources indicate that there isn't a single predictive tool that can tell investors precisely when a stock market downturn will begin, how long it'll last, or how steep the decline will be. But history does conclusively show that these downturns have always represented buying opportunities for optimistic, long-term-minded investors. If the margin debt bubble does burst, opportunity will await.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.
  • Several sellers who had run shops for years noted they were leaving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The newly introduced terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:.

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.

Several sellers who had run shops for years noted they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

Sources indicate that kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

He said third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

According to recent reports, some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after people complained, the Times reported.

The company cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.
  • In a recent development, this White Paper explains these challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

In a recent development, this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

Prediction: This Will Be Micron’s Stock Price by the End of 2028

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few companies have seen their earnings soar amid the artificial intelligence boom like Micron Technology (MU -13.89%).
  • In a recent development, the stock trades for about $690 per share as of this writing, an impressive 201% gain over the past year and a 598% gain over the past 18 months.
  • But as the saying goes, "Past results are not indicative of future returns." Future potential investors need to consider what they can expect from Micron and what that means for the stock price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adam Levy – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:15AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

Few companies have seen their earnings soar amid the artificial intelligence boom like Micron Technology (MU -13.89%). The memory chipmaker has benefited from a spike in demand for its chips, even as it and its competitors take years to ramp up latest supply capacity. The result is eye-popping profit margins and a stock price that's gone parabolic.

In a recent development, the stock trades for about $690 per share as of this writing, an impressive 201% gain over the past year and a 598% gain over the past 18 months. Even so, the stock is about 43% off its all-time high reached over the summer.

But as the saying goes, "Past results are not indicative of future returns." Future potential investors need to consider what they can expect from Micron and what that means for the stock price. Here's my prediction for Micron's stock price by the end of 2028.

Micron's earnings growth is directly tied to its ability to charge extremely high prices for memory, specifically high bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with GPUs and AI accelerators for AI training and inference.

Industry observers note that as a result, Micron's gross margin has climbed to an astonishing 87%. But that pricing isn't indicative of a competitive moat, as many high-gross-margin businesses exhibit. Note that rival chipmaker SK Hynix (SKHY -13.11%) produced a gross margin of 86% in its most recent quarter, practically on par with Micron.

The margin strength stems from the supply/demand imbalance. Micron stated supply constraints will be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026 in its fourth-quarter earnings presentation. That suggests prices could keep climbing through 2028.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Recent findings suggest that SK Hynix suggested that demand could outpace supply through 2030. But just because demand remains higher than supply doesn't mean prices will keep climbing. Demand has to grow faster than supply.

In a recent development, so, investors expecting prices to continue climbing through 2030 may be mistaken. Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung are set to open and ramp up newly introduced production facilities in late 2028.

Sources indicate that so, it's likely pricing peaks in 2028 ahead of the massive ramp-up in production capacity. Earnings could peak in late 2028 or early 2029 as a result.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, as supply constraints ease, prices go down, gross margins decline, and operating costs increase. Once supply reaches equilibrium or exceeds demand, profits can sink swiftly. And given the massive amounts memory chipmakers are spending on new capacity, the next downcycle could lead to a substantial drop in earnings.

It has been revealed that the potential for that drop will affect how much investors are willing to pay for the stock's earnings near the cycle peak. A bigger drop-off in earnings will result in a lower multiple on the stock. Micron and its competitors are working to reduce the cyclicality of their businesses by signing long-term agreements with customers, but that may only delay an earnings decline and make the drop-off worse once those contracts expire.

It has been revealed that as such, investors are unlikely to pay a very high multiple near Micron's peak earnings. Historically, Micron has commanded a multiple of 3-8 times earnings at its peak. With the potential for a large downcycle, shares are likely to trade in the 3-5-times range, with earnings expected to peak in 2028 or 2029.

It's important to note that the stock price usually peaks before earnings peak. Investors are almost always forward-looking. Any hint that pricing is nearing its peak and earnings are set for a near-term downturn will push the stock lower. We saw that happen last month when Sandisk reported disappointing price improvements for its flash memory NAND chips, and the stock dropped after earnings.

In a recent development, with analysts currently expecting $211 per share in earnings for fiscal 2028 and $218 per share for fiscal 2029, that puts my prediction for Micron's stock price at the end of 2028 somewhere between $610 and $1,040. With the stock trading for $690 right now, it doesn't look like a great time to buy unless you think the earnings cycle will last much longer and the drop-off in earnings will be far less severe once earnings peak.

SK Hynix will become Kioxia’s largest shareholder through a bond swap

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.
  • SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares.
  • Industry observers note that bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.

SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.

Industry observers note that bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

Industry observers note that SPC2 is a special-purpose company set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.

Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no newly introduced money, MoneyToday reported, citing the organization. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.

In a recent development, SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.

Both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.

The 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.

Both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson noted its management will stay independent.

“We at the moment have no intends to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official said.

Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.

The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.

According to recent reports, the stake still gives SK Hynix some say over massive decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.

Separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean manufacturer reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

10 stocks we like better than CME Group ›.

Industry observers note that market volatility often creates opportunities for the platforms that facilitate trading. Deciding between CME Group (CME +0.41%) and Robinhood Markets (HOOD -9.44%) involves weighing the stability of an institutional giant against a fast-growing retail disruptor.

CME Group provides the essential infrastructure for global derivatives trading, offering unmatched liquidity to professional investors. Robinhood Markets has transitioned from a simple trading app to a diversified financial services provider for the modern retail investor. Both companies are positioned to benefit from increased market activity but offer different paths for shareholders.

CME Group operates the world's most diverse derivatives marketplace, offering contracts across interest rates, equities, and commodities in 200 countries. Key partnerships include a 10-year agreement with Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) and a prediction market joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT -1.80%). Because one company accounted for roughly 12% of clearing and transaction fees in its latest report, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk.

Industry observers note that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $7 billion, an increase of approximately 9% over the prior period. During this time, net income was roughly $4.4 billion as the firm benefited from increased trading volumes. CME maintains a high net margin of approximately 63.1%, highlighting its strength among financial stocks.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the organization uses very little borrowed money to fund its operations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $4.2 billion, reflecting strong cash conversion from its earnings.

It has been revealed that robinhood Markets provides retail brokerage, advisory, and digital banking services to millions of funded customers. Its platform supports trading in traditional assets as well as Bitcoin (BTC +3.05%). It also operates a joint venture with Susquehanna International Group to run an independent futures exchange and clearinghouse.

In a recent development, in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $5.1 billion, fueled by revenue growth of approximately 21.1%. The organization reported net income of close to $2 billion for the same period, reflecting success in scaling its subscription services and interest-earning assets. Its net margin for this time frame was roughly 39%.

In a recent development, as of Robinhood's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 1.3. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $1.6 billion, showing the manufacturer's ability to generate cash while expanding.

It has been revealed that CME Group faces intense competition from other global exchanges like Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -0.52%) and Nasdaq (NDAQ -0.99%). The manufacturer is also subject to regulatory and legislative changes that could impact its clearinghouse and transaction structures. Furthermore, the company manages operational risks related to third-party data centers, highlighted by a cooling failure in November 2025. Cybersecurity threats targeting financial infrastructure also remain a persistent risk for the exchange operator.

Robinhood Markets is sensitive to regulatory scrutiny regarding payment for order flow, which accounts for a substantial portion of its revenue. It competes with established brokerages like Charles Schwab (SCHW -2.13%) and fintech rivals that may have greater capital and brand recognition. The company also depends on a limited number of liquidity providers, such as Virtu Financial (VIRT -4.76%), to execute its trades. Additionally, legal challenges regarding the offering of event contracts could impact Robinhood's future product road map.

Robinhood Markets is cheaper by its P/S ratio, which measures market cap against sales over the past 12 months, while CME Group has a lower forward P/E.

Sources indicate that I think in a somewhat unsettled market like the one we're right now experiencing, a mature, established operator looks like a more attractive stock. Some investors may prefer growth over consistency, in which case, Robinhood may be more appealing. But for me, CME Group gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.

  • Signal’s latest app patch on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new enhancement that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app patch on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that states: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Sources indicate that fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the new toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

It’s good to see that users can manually disable the newly introduced privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise important questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Recent findings suggest that apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing owners to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this upgrade.

Tech Report: ASML vs. Broadcom: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 9:21AM EST.
  • It has been revealed that the semiconductor world is currently split between the machines that build chips and the designs that power them.
  • ASML holds a virtual monopoly on the advanced lithography machinery required to print the world's most sophisticated microchips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 9:21AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than ASML ›.

It has been revealed that the semiconductor world is currently split between the machines that build chips and the designs that power them. Is ASML (ASML -6.63%) or Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%) the better play for your portfolio?

ASML holds a virtual monopoly on the advanced lithography machinery required to print the world's most sophisticated microchips. Meanwhile, Broadcom has evolved into a powerhouse of networking components and enterprise software. Both companies are critical to the tech supply chain, but they offer distinct paths for investors seeking exposure to high-end silicon.

Recent findings suggest that ASML manufactures lithography systems, which are massive machines that use light to print intricate patterns onto silicon wafers. It provides the essential hardware for every major chipmaker to produce smaller, faster, and more efficient processors. Because its technology is unique, it serves as a critical gatekeeper for the entire high-end semiconductor market.

Sources indicate that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $43.4 billion, an increase of roughly 22.5%. The organization generated approximately $14.8 billion in net income. This growth highlights the sustained demand for extreme ultraviolet lithography systems used in advanced chip production for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

As of ASML's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a organization's ability to cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is approximately 1.3. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2, showing that the company uses relatively little debt compared to its total equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $12.2 billion.

According to recent reports, broadcom is a dominant player among semiconductor stocks, providing infrastructure software and hardware solutions to global enterprises. The tech giant has significant customer concentration, with its top five end customers accounting for roughly 40% of revenue in its latest annual report. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as evidenced by a $30 billion commitment from Apple (AAPL -1.90%).

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached close to $89.1 billion, representing significant growth of nearly 48.7%. The tech giant reported net income of approximately $38.3 billion during this time frame. This surge was partly driven by the integration of large acquisitions and booming demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure across data centers.

Sources indicate that as of Broadcom's November 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 1.7. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.8, indicating a higher level of total debt relative to shareholder equity than ASML. In the fiscal year ended Nov. 2, 2025, free cash flow was close to $26.9 billion, though stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

ASML faces risks from its position at the center of global trade tensions, particularly concerning international export restrictions. The company also operates in the cyclical semiconductor equipment market, where spending by chipmakers can fluctuate based on broader economic conditions and interest rates. Furthermore, the rapid pace of innovation requires constant, heavy investment in research and development to maintain its technological lead over any potential competitors.

Broadcom operates in a highly cyclical industry that faces rapid price erosion and evolving technological requirements driven by artificial intelligence. It relies heavily on a limited number of contract manufacturers, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM -9.48%), which produced approximately 95% of its wafers according to its latest annual report. Broadcom also faces intense regulatory scrutiny and risks associated with its strategy of integrating large acquisitions into its software portfolio.

Broadcom looks potentially cheaper based on its forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, whereas ASML has a lower P/S ratio.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The current market environment is, shall we say, hostile to tech stocks, and shares of ASML and Broadcom reflect that:.

That said, zooming out over the past decade, both stocks have put in decent performances, handily outpacing the S&P 500's (^GSPC -3.70%) return:.

In a recent development, in the past, I have picked ASML over many other stocks for several reasons. For one, it has a monopoly in the extreme ultraviolet lithography niche it operates in. That gives it strong pricing power and a solid moat. ASML also consistently reports a net margin in excess of 30%, and it pays a modest dividend.

However, it's hard to argue with Broadcom's long-term performance. A organization of that size reporting nearly 50% revenue growth is pretty wild. ASML and Broadcom are both exposed to the inherent cyclicality of the semiconductor industry, so I think that risk factor offsets itself. And the tech sector (and the market in general) may be melting down right now, but long-term investors shouldn't get especially concerned over what happens in the course of a week, or a month, or even a year.

I'm breaking with my pattern here. I don't think ASML is a bad choice, to be clear, but Broadcom has strong margins and even better revenue growth. Broadcom gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.
